blocks.text: 24. Colonial and Capitalistic Perspectives of Gender

segments.text: This topic examines how colonialism and the spread of capitalism reshaped gender roles in colonised societies, often worsening women’s economic and social position rather than being neutral processes.
Colonial impact on gender roles.

Pre-colonial societies in many parts of Africa and Asia had women actively involved in agriculture, trade, and local decision-making, with rights to land and resources that varied by community but were often more substantial than colonial administrators assumed. Colonial administrations, importing Victorian-era European assumptions that women belonged in the domestic sphere and men in public economic and political life, frequently restructured land ownership, taxation, and cash-crop farming systems to register land and issue formal legal and economic status to men as household heads, systematically excluding women from the formal economy and land rights they had previously exercised informally.
Capitalism’s role.

As colonial and later independent economies were drawn into global capitalist markets (Topic 14’s Marxist feminist framework applies directly here), the demand for cheap, flexible labour created strong incentives to keep women’s labour informal and underpaid — as unpaid family labour on cash crops, or as low-wage factory labour in export industries — while formal wage employment, unionisation, and property rights were disproportionately available to men.
Why this matters for development theory.

This colonial and capitalist history is the essential background for understanding the development theories that follow (Topics 25–27) and the WID/WAD/GAD policy frameworks (Topics 29–31): development economists in the 1970s began to recognise that women had often been worse off after colonial-era economic integration and modernisation than before it, directly challenging the assumption that economic development automatically benefits everyone, including women, equally.
Key Takeaways

items.text: Colonial administration often replaced women’s pre-existing informal land and economic rights with formal systems that recognised only men as economic actors.
Capitalist integration created incentives to keep women’s labour cheap and informal, echoing Marxist feminist analysis (Topic 14).
This history motivated the recognition that development is not gender-neutral, directly shaping later WID/WAD/GAD frameworks.

segments.text: Modernization theory, dominant in development economics through the 1950s–1960s, argued that “underdeveloped” societies would develop by following the same path already taken by industrialised Western nations — moving from traditional agrarian economies to modern industrial ones through capital investment, technology transfer, and the adoption of modern social and economic institutions.
Gender assumptions within modernization theory.

The theory generally assumed that development’s benefits (education, formal employment, higher incomes) would “trickle down” to women automatically as a society modernised, and paid little explicit attention to how development projects affected men and women differently. Where women were considered at all, it was often through a narrow lens focused on reducing fertility rates and improving women’s roles as mothers, rather than as independent economic actors.
Feminist critique.

Ester Boserup’s landmark study Women’s Role in Economic Development (1970) directly challenged modernization theory by showing empirically that development projects — introducing new agricultural technology, cash crops, and mechanisation — frequently bypassed women farmers (who in many African contexts did the bulk of subsistence food production) in favour of men, who were given the training, credit, and modern equipment, actually worsening women’s relative economic position and workload even as overall production increased. Boserup’s work is widely credited as the founding text of what became the Women in Development (WID) approach (Topic 29).
Why examiners test this.

It illustrates a recurring theme across this entire section (V): treating development as gender-neutral is itself a form of gender bias, because existing gender inequalities determine who actually captures the benefits of new resources, technology, and income, even when policy does not explicitly discriminate.
Key Takeaways

items.text: Modernization theory assumed development benefits would trickle down to women automatically, without addressing gender differences explicitly.
Boserup’s 1970 study showed development projects often bypassed women farmers, worsening their relative position — the foundational critique behind WID.
Core lesson: gender-neutral development policy is not automatically gender-equal in its outcomes.

segments.text: World System Theory, developed by Immanuel Wallerstein, analyses global economic inequality not as a matter of individual countries being at different “stages” of development (as modernization theory assumed) but as the product of a single, integrated global capitalist economy structured into a hierarchy of “core” (wealthy, industrialised), “periphery” (poor, primarily resource- and labour-exporting), and “semi-periphery” nations, in which the core systematically extracts wealth from the periphery through unequal trade and investment relationships.
Gendered dimension.

Applied to gender, World System Theory highlights how peripheral countries’ integration into the global economy relies heavily on cheap, feminised labour — export-processing zones and garment or electronics factories in periphery and semi-periphery countries (including Pakistan, Bangladesh, and other South and Southeast Asian countries) disproportionately employ women at low wages, with limited labour protections, because a large, socially undervalued female workforce is precisely what allows peripheral economies to compete for footloose international capital seeking the cheapest possible production costs.
Distinctive contribution to gender-and-development debates.

Unlike modernization theory, which located the “problem” within individual traditional societies needing to modernise, World System Theory locates the problem in the structure of the global economy itself, implying that women’s disadvantage in periphery countries cannot be solved simply by internal reform or more development aid, but requires addressing structurally unequal terms of global trade and capital flows.
Criticism.

Critics argue the theory can be overly deterministic, treating peripheral countries’ economic roles as almost entirely fixed by the global system, leaving comparatively little room to explain successful cases of economic transformation (such as some East Asian economies) achieved by former periphery states, or to explain internal variation in gender outcomes among periphery countries with similar positions in the global economy.
Key Takeaways

items.text: World System Theory (Wallerstein) explains global inequality through core-periphery-semi-periphery structure within one integrated capitalist world economy.
Peripheral economies’ reliance on cheap, feminised export labour (e.g., garment industries) is the theory’s key gendered insight.
Criticised as overly deterministic, underexplaining cases of successful economic transformation by former periphery states.

segments.text: Dependency Theory, closely related to World System Theory but developed earlier (primarily by Latin American economists such as Raúl Prebisch and later scholars like Andre Gunder Frank, from the 1950s–1960s), argues that “underdeveloped” countries are not simply behind on a universal development path (as modernization theory claimed) but have been actively made poor — their development has been distorted and constrained — by their historical and ongoing economic relationship with wealthier, more powerful countries, first through colonialism and later through unequal trade, debt, and multinational investment relationships.
Mechanism.

Dependency theorists argue that periphery countries are locked into exporting raw materials and agricultural commodities (whose prices are volatile and, over the long term, tend to decline relative to the price of manufactured goods they must import), which prevents them from accumulating the capital needed to industrialise and develop more diversified, self-sufficient economies — a state of structural “dependency” on the core.
Gendered application.

Applied to gender, dependency theory highlights how structural adjustment programmes and export-oriented growth strategies imposed on dependent economies (often as conditions attached to international loans, discussed further in Topic 32) tend to cut public spending on health, education, and social services — cuts that disproportionately increase women’s unpaid care burden, since women are typically expected to compensate for reduced state provision of care services within the household.
Relationship to World System Theory.

The two theories are often taught together because they share the core claim that global economic structure, not internal national characteristics, is the primary cause of underdevelopment; World System Theory offers a more elaborate three-tier global structure, while Dependency Theory focuses more specifically on the mechanisms (trade terms, capital flight, debt) that keep periphery economies dependent.
Key Takeaways

items.text: Dependency Theory argues periphery countries are made poor by structurally unequal relationships with core countries, not merely “behind” on a universal path.
Reliance on raw-material exports with declining relative value traps dependent economies in a cycle preventing industrialisation.
Gendered link: dependency-driven austerity and structural adjustment disproportionately shift care burdens onto women (connects to Topic 32).

segments.text: Structural functionalism is a sociological theory (associated with Talcott Parsons) that predates and stands in contrast to the critical development theories above. It explains social institutions, including the gendered division of labour within the family, by asking what social “function” they serve in maintaining the stability of the overall social system, rather than asking who benefits or loses power.
Parsons’s account of gender roles.

Parsons argued that the mid-twentieth-century nuclear family divided labour efficiently between an “instrumental” role (typically assigned to the husband — earning income and dealing with the world outside the family) and an “expressive” role (typically assigned to the wife — providing emotional support and managing internal family relationships and childcare), and that this division of labour was functional because it minimised role conflict and helped the family unit run smoothly, which in turn stabilised the broader society that depends on well-functioning families to raise the next generation of productive members.
Why feminist theory rejects this account.

Feminist critics point out several serious problems: the theory treats a historically and culturally specific arrangement (the mid-century Western nuclear family, with a male breadwinner and female homemaker) as if it were a universal, natural, and efficient functional necessity, when in fact this arrangement is neither universal across cultures nor historically constant even within the West. It also treats the division of labour as harmoniously agreed upon and mutually beneficial, ignoring the unequal power, unequal pay, and restricted choices this arrangement actually imposed on women, who were expected to remain in the “expressive” role regardless of individual preference or talent. Because functionalism asks only “does this arrangement help the system run smoothly?” rather than “is this arrangement fair, and who benefits from it?”, it structurally cannot identify or critique gender inequality — a fundamental theoretical weakness from a feminist standpoint.
Why the theory is still taught.

It is included in the syllabus specifically as a contrast case: understanding functionalism’s blind spot toward power and inequality is what makes the feminist and conflict-oriented critiques (from Topics 12–17, 26, 27) analytically sharper by comparison.
Key Takeaways

items.text: Structural functionalism (Parsons) explains gender roles by their supposed function in maintaining family and social stability, not by questions of power or fairness.
The classic instrumental (male)/expressive (female) role division is presented as functionally efficient, not as historically specific or unequal.
Feminist critique: functionalism cannot identify inequality because it does not ask who benefits and who is constrained by a given social arrangement.

segments.text: Women in Development (WID) was the first major policy framework (emerging in the early-to-mid 1970s, directly following Boserup’s 1970 critique discussed in Topic 25) through which international development institutions explicitly began addressing women in their programming, rather than assuming development was gender-neutral.
Core approach.

WID’s central strategy was to integrate women more fully into existing development processes — by giving women better access to credit, agricultural training, technology, and income-generating projects — on the theory that women had simply been left out of development so far, and that including them within existing development models would improve outcomes both for women and for overall economic growth (“efficiency” argument).
Strengths.

WID succeeded in making women’s economic contribution visible to policymakers for the first time in a systematic way, and led to concrete programming — women-specific microcredit schemes, agricultural extension programmes targeted at women farmers, and income-generation projects — that produced real, measurable benefits in many contexts.
Criticism, which directly motivated the next frameworks (Topics 30–31).

Critics argued that WID treated women as a separate, add-on category to be integrated into an unchanged, male-defined development model, rather than questioning why the model excluded women in the first place, or examining the underlying gender relations (unequal power, unpaid domestic labour, restricted decision-making authority) that caused women’s exclusion. It also tended to add income-generating responsibilities onto women’s existing unpaid domestic workload without addressing that workload, increasing women’s total labour burden — sometimes called the “triple burden” of productive, reproductive, and community work.
Key Takeaways

items.text: WID (1970s) sought to integrate women into existing development processes through targeted access to credit, training, and income projects.
Its main strength was making women’s economic role newly visible to policymakers.
Main criticism: it added responsibilities onto women without addressing unpaid domestic labour or underlying gender power relations, motivating WAD and GAD.

segments.text: Women and Development (WAD), emerging in the late 1970s largely from Marxist and dependency-theory-influenced scholars (Topics 14, 27), responded to WID’s central weakness by arguing that women had never actually been “left out” of development at all — they had always been integrated into economic processes, but on unequal and exploitative terms, particularly through unpaid reproductive labour and underpaid informal work.
Core argument.

WAD’s key claim is that the problem is not women’s exclusion from development, but the exploitative structure of the development process itself — the same global capitalist and patriarchal structures analysed in dependency theory and Marxist feminism. On this view, simply adding women more fully into existing development programmes (the WID solution) cannot fix the problem, because the structure of the global economy itself, not merely women’s absence from it, is what generates inequality.
Comparison with WID.

Where WID asks “how can we integrate women better into development?”, WAD asks “why does the existing development model exploit women’s labour, and how must that model itself change?” WAD is therefore more structurally critical and less optimistic that simply adding targeted women’s projects within an unchanged system will solve the underlying problem.
Limitation of WAD.

Critics note that WAD, by focusing heavily on structural, class-based, and international economic explanations, sometimes underplayed the importance of gender relations within the household and local community (patriarchal power dynamics between husbands and wives, for example) as a cause of inequality distinct from global capitalism — a gap the next framework, GAD, was designed to close.
Key Takeaways

items.text: WAD (late 1970s) argues women were always integrated into development, but on exploitative terms, not excluded from it.
It locates the cause of inequality in the structure of the global capitalist development process itself, not women’s absence from programmes.
Its limitation: underemphasises household-level patriarchal power relations, a gap GAD later addressed.

segments.text: Gender and Development (GAD), emerging in the 1980s, is generally regarded as the most theoretically comprehensive of the three frameworks (WID, WAD, GAD), because it combines WAD’s structural critique of the global economy with explicit attention to gender relations of power within households, communities, and institutions — the piece WAD had underemphasised.
Core shift in focus.

Rather than focusing narrowly on “women” as a target group (as WID did) or purely on global economic structures (as WAD did), GAD analyses the social relations between men and women — how power, resources, and responsibilities are divided between genders at every level, from the household to international institutions — and asks how development interventions can transform unequal gender relations rather than simply working around them.
Key conceptual tools introduced by GAD:

items.text: Practical needs vs. strategic needs

(a distinction developed by Maxine Molyneux and taken up widely in GAD): practical gender needs are immediate, material needs arising from women’s existing roles (for example, a nearby water source to reduce time spent fetching water); strategic gender needs address the underlying unequal power relations that created those roles in the first place (for example, changing land inheritance laws so women can own property independently). GAD emphasises that development should aim to address strategic needs, not only practical ones, or existing inequality will simply be managed rather than reduced.
Gender mainstreaming

(Topic 4, Topic 22) — the idea that gender analysis should be integrated into every policy area, not confined to separate women’s projects, is the operational strategy most closely associated with GAD and was formally adopted by the UN at the 1995 Beijing Conference.

segments.text: Why GAD is considered the dominant current framework.

Most contemporary international development institutions (the UN, World Bank, major bilateral donors) officially frame their gender policy in GAD terms — emphasising gender relations, mainstreaming, and strategic needs — even though WID-style targeted women’s projects continue to operate in practice alongside GAD’s broader framework.
Key Takeaways

items.text: GAD (1980s) combines WAD’s structural critique with explicit analysis of gender power relations within households and institutions.
Molyneux’s practical needs/strategic needs distinction is GAD’s key conceptual tool; addressing strategic needs is necessary to change underlying inequality.
Gender mainstreaming (adopted at Beijing 1995) is GAD’s dominant operational strategy and remains the mainstream international policy framework today.

segments.text: Structural Adjustment Programmes (SAPs) were economic reform packages imposed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank as conditions attached to loans to heavily indebted developing countries, especially from the 1980s onward, typically requiring recipient governments to cut public spending, reduce subsidies, privatise state enterprises, devalue currency, and orient the economy toward export-led growth.
Gendered impact — the mechanism.

Feminist economists, building on dependency theory (Topic 27) and GAD analysis (Topic 31), demonstrated that SAPs, although presented as gender-neutral macroeconomic policy, had systematically different effects on men and women:

items.text: Cuts to public health and education spending

shifted the burden of care (nursing sick family members, home-schooling, fetching water where public services were cut) onto women’s unpaid labour, since someone still had to perform this work even after the state stopped funding it.
Removal of food and fuel subsidies
increased the time and effort women spent managing household budgets and food provision, since women were typically responsible for stretching reduced household resources.
Export-oriented growth strategies

increased demand for women’s cheap factory labour (as in the World System Theory analysis, Topic 26) even as public support services that could have eased women’s domestic burden were being cut, effectively increasing women’s total workload across both paid and unpaid spheres simultaneously.

segments.text: Why this became a landmark feminist economics critique.

This body of research, associated particularly with economists like Diane Elson, was highly influential because it demonstrated with concrete empirical detail that macroeconomic policy is never actually gender-neutral — it has systematically different, and often more burdensome, effects on women — even though mainstream economic policy analysis at the time rarely considered gender at all.
Contemporary relevance.

This critique remains directly relevant to Pakistan’s recurring IMF programmes, where similar debates continue about whether fiscal austerity conditions disproportionately burden women through cuts to public health and education spending and increases in the cost of living.
Key Takeaways

items.text: SAPs (1980s onward) required austerity, privatisation, and export orientation as loan conditions from the IMF/World Bank.
Feminist economists (e.g., Diane Elson) showed SAPs systematically shifted burdens onto women through cuts to public services and rising unpaid care work.
The critique remains directly relevant to contemporary IMF programmes in countries like Pakistan.

segments.text: Globalization — the accelerating international integration of trade, capital, labour, and communication — has produced complex and sometimes contradictory effects on gender relations, which is why this topic requires a genuinely two-sided analysis rather than a one-directional “good” or “bad” verdict.
Ways globalization has been argued to benefit women:

items.text: Export-oriented manufacturing jobs

(garments, electronics) have drawn large numbers of women into paid employment in many developing countries, including Pakistan, giving some women independent income and greater household bargaining power for the first time, even though these jobs are frequently low-paid and precarious (linking back to Topics 26 and 32).
Global information and communication technologies

have expanded women’s access to education, information about their legal rights, and networks with international and local women’s rights organisations, strengthening feminist advocacy and cross-border solidarity movements.
Global norm diffusion

— international treaties and conferences (Topic 22) and global media exposure to different gender norms have pressured many governments, including Pakistan’s, to reform discriminatory laws and adopt international gender-equality standards.

segments.text: Ways globalization has been argued to harm women:

items.text: The “race to the bottom” in labour standards

, where countries compete for foreign investment partly by offering cheap, poorly protected labour, has meant that much of the new employment available to women comes with low wages, minimal job security, and weak enforcement of labour rights.
Global economic volatility
(financial crises, commodity price swings) disproportionately affects the informal and precarious jobs many women hold, with fewer protections than in the formal sector.
Human trafficking and exploitative labour migration

, a serious concern in gender-and-globalization literature, has expanded alongside globalization’s increased cross-border labour mobility, disproportionately victimising women and children in specific sectors such as domestic work and the sex trade.

segments.text: Balanced conclusion for exam purposes.

The evidence does not support a single verdict; globalization has expanded some forms of women’s economic participation and rights awareness while simultaneously exposing many women to new forms of precarious labour and exploitation, and the actual outcome in a given country depends heavily on domestic labour law, enforcement capacity, and social protection systems.
Key Takeaways

items.text: Globalization has expanded women’s paid employment and rights awareness through export industries, ICT access, and international norm diffusion.
It has also intensified precarious, poorly protected labour and cross-border exploitation, including trafficking.
The net effect depends on domestic labour regulation and enforcement, not on globalization alone.
